newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Aleman confirmed as president-elect of Nicaragua.
newsitem.headline: Aleman confirmed as president-elect of Nicaragua.

text.p: Nicaragua's Supreme Electoral Council late on Friday confirmed right-wing President-elect Arnoldo Aleman's victory in Oct. 20 elections, rejecting an appeal for new voting by the rival left-wing Sandinista Front.
"After a revision of the vote, we conclude that ... Arnoldo Aleman was elected president," Rosa Marina Zelaya, president of the Supreme Electoral Council (CSE), told a news conference.
Aleman defeated former president and Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega by 51 percent to 37.7 percent in provisional results released by the council about two weeks ago, some 17 days after the election.
But Ortega refused to concede defeat, alleging fraud in Managua and Matagalpa departments (provinces) and demanding new voting there.
"We duly reviewed the tally sheets and concluded that the elections in Managua and Matagalpa were perfectly valid," Zelaya said.
She said final vote figures in the presidential race, which could change slightly from the provisional numbers, would be released next week.

There was no immediate reaction from Ortega or the Sandinistas, but political analysts have warned of unrest from Sandinista supporters, many of whom believe the elections were stolen from them by Liberal fraud.

At Aleman's jubilant Liberal Alliance headquarters in Managua early on Saturday, the portly president-elect extended an olive branch to the Sandinistas, offering to work with them after he takes office on Jan. 10.

"Here, today, I make a call to Comandante Daniel Ortega that for the sake of Nicaragua together we make the transformations so that the dispossessed classes no longer must bear the suffering and poverty," Aleman told a news conference.
Liberal officials said they hoped the announcement would end the nasty post-election squabbling that had threatened Nicaragua's stability and sullied its new democratic image.
"Now, finally these elections are over and the time to get to work has arrived," the Liberal Mayor-elect of Managua, Roberto Cedeno, told reporters.

Foreign election observers like former U.S. President Jimmy Carter called the voting flawed but fair and expressed confidence in the results. U.S. President Bill Clinton and other world leaders had already congratulated Aleman.
Earlier on Friday, Aleman said he would ask to meet with Ortega once Ortega recognises his victory.

Ortega has said he will recognise the "legality" but not the "legitimacy" of a future Aleman government, and he said there could be a deepening political crisis if the CSE upheld the results as preliminarily reported.
